analysis.one_liner: Sets federal consumer protections and financial penalties for managed care health plans covering millions.
analysis.headline: The Managed Care Consumer Protection Act of 1997 was introduced in January 1997 with 27 cosponsors but never received a vote, dying in the Ways and Means and Commerce committees.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have required HMOs and other managed care health plans to meet federal standards for approving and denying care, covering emergencies, providing minimum hospital stays after childbirth, and disclosing how doctors are paid. It would enforce those rules with a 25% excise tax on a plan's premiums for noncompliance, and would tighten protections for Medicare and Medicaid beneficiaries in managed care, including guaranteed access to supplemental (Medigap) coverage without health-based price discrimination.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary Americans enrolled in managed care plans, including Medicare and Medicaid beneficiaries, who faced care denials, restricted access to specialists and emergency rooms, and 'drive-through' deliveries; women giving birth, people with chronic illnesses, and seniors relying on Medigap policies gain enforceable rights.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Managed care enrollees, Medicare and Medicaid beneficiaries

how_it_helps.text: Imposes an excise tax equal to 25% of a plan's premiums if the plan fails to meet federal beneficiary-protection requirements, giving the standards real financial teeth [S2] [S3].

Bars plans from denying coverage through utilization review unless the program meets Health and Human Services standards, and prohibits paying utilization reviewers based on the number of coverage denials [S2].
Requires plans to cover emergency services without prior authorization and without penalizing care from out-of-network providers, and to use a 'prudent layperson' standard for emergencies [S2] [S3].
Mandates minimum hospital stays of 48 hours after vaginal delivery and 96 hours after cesarean section, with covered post-delivery follow-up care if discharge comes earlier [S2] [S3].

Requires plans to assure timely access to a sufficient number and variety of providers, direct access to OB-GYNs without a referral, access to specialists and centers of excellence for chronic conditions, and coverage of care in approved clinical trials [S2] [S3].

Protects doctor-patient communication: plans cannot gag physicians from discussing treatment options, denial criteria, or financial incentives, and cannot retaliate against doctors who speak up [S2] [S3].

Strengthens Medigap protections: raises the required loss ratio from 75% to 85% of premiums, requires guaranteed issue without preexisting-condition exclusions for people losing other coverage, and opens annual enrollment periods free of health-based pricing [S2].

Creates an Office of Medicare Advocacy for independent review of beneficiary problems, requires annual comparative information on Medicare managed care plans, and excludes plans from Medicare and Medicaid if they submit false quality data [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Managed care insurers and HMOs, who would face new federal requirements and a 25%-of-premiums excise tax for violations, plus the administrative cost of grievance procedures, disclosures, and credentialing standards; costs could be passed to premiums.

drawbacks.text: Enforcing the standards through a 25% excise tax on premiums is a heavy blunt penalty that could raise compliance costs and push some premiums upward, which would ultimately reach consumers [S3].

Federal requirements layered on top of state insurance regulation can create duplicated oversight and compliance burdens, and several provisions would depend on detailed rulemaking by the Secretary of Health and Human Services [S2] [S3].

Mandated minimum benefits and access standards can limit plans' ability to manage costs, and opponents argued such federal mandates would raise health costs for employers and consumers — the core policy dispute that later shaped the patients' bill of rights debate (general knowledge).

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For the millions of Americans in managed care plans in the late 1990s, the bill's concrete protections — emergency care without prior authorization, minimum post-delivery stays, an end to denial-based reviewer bonuses, and real penalties for violations — addressed widely documented harms of the era. The main cost is higher premiums and administrative burden for plans, some of which would reach consumers; the 25% excise tax is a strong enforcement tool but a blunt one. The record shows no floor debate or amendments refining these tradeoffs, because the bill never advanced past referral.

outcome.mechanism: Introduced on January 7, 1997 and referred to the Ways and Means and Commerce committees; subcommittee referrals on January 21 and 27, 1997 were its last actions, and no markup or vote ever occurred before the 105th Congress ended [S1] [S5].

narrative.text: Rep. Pete Stark introduced the bill on January 7, 1997, joined by 27 cosponsors — 26 Democrats and Independent Bernard Sanders [S1] [S4] [S5].

The bill was referred to both the Ways and Means Committee and the Commerce Committee, then to their Health subcommittees in late January 1997; no further action appears in the record for the rest of the Congress [S1] [S5].
Neither committee ever reported the bill, and it never received a floor vote in the House or Senate before the 105th Congress expired in January 1999 [S1] [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Managed care insurers and HMOs are better off because the bill died: none of its consumer-protection requirements or the 25% premium excise tax for noncompliance ever took effect. Working Americans in managed care, including Medicare and Medicaid beneficiaries, gained nothing from the federal protections it promised; their strongest protections arrived only years later through state laws and a narrower federal patients' bill of rights effort in 1998 that the Republican leadership also kept from a House vote (general knowledge).

sides.party_line_note: All 27 cosponsors were Democrats or the one Independent, and the bill never reached a floor vote, so the record shows no partisan roll-call and no Republicans publicly for or against it in the sources; a Republican, Rep. Lewis of Georgia, did join in introducing it [S3] [S4].

industries.note: The bill directly regulated HMOs: certifiable utilization review standards, emergency and maternity coverage mandates, grievance and appeal rights, disclosure of physician incentive plans and executive pay, and a 25%-of-premiums excise tax for violations. Defeating it preserved the plans' discretion to deny care without federal penalty.

The bill would raise their required loss ratio from 75% to 85%, force guaranteed issue without preexisting-condition exclusions for people losing other coverage, and ban health-based pricing — reducing underwriting profits while bringing new guaranteed customers.

Doctors gain anti-gag and anti-retaliation protections, due-process rights against network termination, and bans on denial-count-based reviewer bonuses; but they face new contracting standards and review-participation obligations.
